source.title: The Capabilities and Limitations of Weak-to-Strong Generalization: Generalization and Calibration
source.authors: Wei Yao; Wen-Kai Yang; Geng-Ze Xu; Ziqiao Wang; Yankai Lin; Yong Liu

record.file_problem: Full paper text, including appendices, is present. Some mathematical notation is imperfectly extracted, but the document is not cut off or the wrong document.
record.tranche_reason: It tests weak-to-strong generalization with a different task and performance measures from the original: binary preference accuracy and theoretical KL-divergence bounds, rather than reporting PGR.
record.gate_note: The paper does not calculate PGR explicitly. Results from cited studies are not recorded. The paper does not test auxiliary confidence losses, ensembling weak supervisors, or loss variants as improvements over naive fine-tuning. Calibration findings are recorded but do not directly measure a version's named performance-gap outcome.
record.test_reason: The study derives bounds on when a weakly supervised student beats its teacher (V5) and runs W2SG with GPT-2 and Pythia on CAI-Harmless preference classification. It varies teacher capacity (V3) and training epochs, where longer training pushes accuracy toward or below the teacher (V1/V4). It adds synthetic MLP checks of the bounds. PGR is never computed.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right but incomplete. The authors conclude that student performance is bounded above and below by teacher error and teacher-student disagreement. So weak-model quality matters, and minimizing disagreement limits how far the student can surpass the teacher. Excessive training overfits weak labels, and calibration is inherited from the teacher. Under convexity and realizability assumptions, KL-trained students beat teachers by at least their disagreement.
record.recipe_differences: Uses weak-model predictions to train stronger models, but studies binary preference classification with KL loss and reports accuracy and theoretical KL bounds rather than Burns et al.'s PGR measure. The empirical setup uses relatively small GPT-2 and Pythia models.
record.method_sensitivity: Teacher capacity changes reported generalization; stronger students tend to have larger ECE under the same teacher; increasing weak-label training epochs reduces accuracy and ECE and can make GPT-2-XL perform below its teacher.

fits_no_version.finding: Student ECE is bounded by teacher ECE plus a disagreement term (Theorem 4.2). Stronger students show higher ECE, and longer training moves ECE toward the teacher's.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Under weak supervision, student calibration is inherited from the teacher and degrades with student capacity.

record.problems: The empirical evaluation is limited to two model series and a binary preference task, which the authors describe as relatively small-scale. Empirical results are presented in plots without tabulated per-model values or reported experimental error bars. PGR is not calculated. The paper itself notes that its theoretical assumptions may not match real-world LLM deployment.
record.rows_left_out: No results omitted under the 60-row limit. Calibration results are included as related findings but are not linked to a claim-version verdict because they do not measure performance-gap recovery.

untested.parts: PGR is not computed. Only small GPT-2/Pythia models on one binary preference task, and the text never states student-versus-teacher accuracy at the default one epoch.
All of it: no auxiliary confidence loss, ensembling or loss-variant comparison against naive fine-tuning.
Student size versus accuracy (beyond calibration), task variation (chess, reward-modelling breadth) and representation-based predictors of PGR.
Exploiting what the supervisor can't check, distribution shift, and directly measured weak/strong error correlation.
All of it: no vision experiments.

missing.what: Theorem 4.1 two-sided bound: |student error − teacher error| ≤ O(sqrt(disagreement)). It limits how far the student can exceed the teacher, which the authors frame as a paradox with the training objective.
Corollary B.2: finite-sample forward-KL guarantee under the WIS assumption.
Default 1-epoch W2SG accuracies versus weak-teacher accuracy and strong ceiling, which are needed to compute PGR. Figure 1 only.

record.verdict_notes: Mostly a theory paper. The empirical LM evidence is figure-only, with no error bars and only small models. Calibration rows are correctly excluded from versions. Linking the overfitting results to V4 is an interpretation: the paper frames them as overfitting to weak supervision, not as error correlation.

versions.untested_parts: PGR is not calculated. Empirical tests use binary preference accuracy on CAI-Harmless; the paper does not test the full range of tasks or larger models.
No auxiliary confidence loss, ensemble of weak supervisors, or loss-variant comparison against naive fine-tuning.
Tests model-capacity trends in the GPT-2 and Pythia series on one binary preference task, but not multiple task domains, languages, or representation predictors of PGR.
Tests increased training epochs and overfitting to weak supervision. Does not test distribution shift, exploiting what a supervisor cannot check, or the effect of weak/strong error correlation.
Provides theoretical conditions and synthetic validation for KL-based settings, not a universal condition across losses and model classes.
No vision experiments; vision weak-to-strong work is cited only.

rows.subject: Theorem 5.1, realizable setting
rows.operation_detail: Derives a population-risk bound for weak-to-strong training with reverse KL under realizability and a convex strong task class.

conditions.value: strong ceiling is realizable in the strong model class; convex task class

rows.measure: Strong-model true error relative to weak-model true error and student-supervisor disagreement
rows.baseline: Weak model true error: dP(F⋆, Fw).
rows.value: dP(F⋆, Fsw) ≤ dP(F⋆, Fw) − dP(Fsw, Fw).
rows.note: The stated improvement guarantee is conditional on the theorem's assumptions.
rows.check: This is a theorem, not an empirical test of V1, so V1 is dropped.

rows.subject: Theorem 5.2, non-realizable setting
rows.operation_detail: Derives a finite-sample bound for reverse-KL weak-to-strong training.

conditions.value: convex strong task class; non-realizable setting; n i.i.d. weakly labelled samples

rows.measure: Strong-model true error relative to weak-model error, disagreement, and finite-sample/non-realizability terms
rows.baseline: Weak model true error: dP(F⋆, Fw).
rows.value: dP(F⋆, F̂sw) ≤ dP(F⋆, Fw) − dP(F̂sw, Fw) + O(√ε) + O(√(CFs/n)) + O(√(log(1/δ)/n)).
rows.uncertainty: Probability at least 1 − δ; asymptotics stated as ε → 0 and n → ∞.
rows.note: The finite-sample and non-realizability terms qualify the improvement guarantee.
rows.check: Drop V1 (theorem). The guarantee holds only up to non-realizability and finite-sample terms.

rows.subject: Corollary B.1, realizable setting
rows.operation_detail: Derives a forward-KL guarantee under an additional weighted Itakura–Saito divergence assumption.

conditions.value: realizability, convex strong task class, and DWIS(F⋆∥Fsw) ≤ 0 with weight w = Fsw − Fw

rows.measure: Strong-model true error relative to weak-model true error and disagreement
rows.baseline: Weak model true error: dP(Fw, F⋆).
rows.value: dP(Fsw, F⋆) ≤ dP(Fw, F⋆) − dP(Fw, Fsw).
rows.note: The authors state that the additional assumption is not universally guaranteed, so the result is conditional.
rows.check: Drop V1 (theorem). The extra weighted Itakura–Saito condition is, in the authors' words, not guaranteed to hold.

For this study: Figure 2 compares epochs 1 and 3; accuracy declines with increased training; GPT-2-XL falls below GPT-2-Base's 90.95%.

statements.problem: There is no individually attributable result for this study in this statement. Catalog-wide counts, author overlap and comparisons among other studies cannot be verified from this study's text.

statements.correction: Theorem 5.1: dP(F⋆,Fsw) ≤ dP(F⋆,Fw) − dP(Fsw,Fw), under convexity and realizability. Theorem 5.2 adds non-realizability and finite-sample terms. Figure 3(a): strong representation equals the 16-layer ground truth. Figure 3(b): strong representation is an 8-layer MLP. Figure 3(c): strong representation is a perturbed 16-layer ground-truth MLP. Reverse-KL points cluster around y = x.
statements.problem: The reverse-KL bounds and qualitative synthetic result are correct, but the blanket description of R20–R22 as using 8-layer representations is wrong.

statements.correction: Corollary B.1 requires DWIS(F⋆∥Fsw) ≤ 0 with weight Fsw − Fw; the authors state that this condition is not universally guaranteed. Theorem 4.1 bounds the absolute student–teacher error gap by O(√disagreement).
Reverse KL: improvement bound under convexity and realizability. Forward KL: additional weighted Itakura–Saito condition. Section 5.3 reports points near y = x for both losses.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: The theoretical KL settings and synthetic experiments under their stated assumptions
reader_labels.reason: The bounds guarantee an error reduction tied to weak-strong disagreement, and the synthetic results report improvement approximately matching disagreement (R17-R25).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: More weak-label training epochs in the tested Pythia and GPT-2 students
reader_labels.reason: Accuracy declines toward the weak teacher's performance as training increases, indicating that weak-to-strong gains are incomplete and training-dependent (R5-R9).

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.reason: The authors state that its accuracy falls below the GPT-2-Base teacher's 90.95% accuracy (R10).

reader_labels.label: supports

reader_labels.reason: For a given student, the authors report better generalization with a higher-capacity weak teacher (R1-R2).
